one_liner: JIT GPU kernel generator for e3nn-style Clebsch-Gordan tensor products and fused graph convolutions; claims up to 10x over e3nn.
what_it_does: It replaces e3nn's o3.TensorProduct for the 'uvu' and 'uvw' connection modes used in equivariant interatomic-potential GNNs (MACE, NequIP, Nequix, SevenNet, DiffDock) with kernels generated at run time for CUDA, HIP and, in beta, SYCL. You describe the product with oeq.TPProblem, which nearly mirrors o3.TensorProduct but requires internal_weights=False, then call oeq.TensorProduct(problem, torch_op=True)(X, Y, W). oeq.TensorProductConv fuses the tensor product with the message-passing scatter-sum over an edge index. There are PyTorch and JAX frontends, with backward, double and triple backward in PyTorch, JVP in JAX, and support for torch.compile, torch.export and AOTInductor.
how_it_is_fast: It exploits the sparsity of the Clebsch-Gordan (Wigner 3j) coefficient tensor. At JIT time the generator enumerates the nonzeros and writes them as hex float literals into fully unrolled CUDA/HIP code from Jinja templates (ComputationSchedule.py, loop_unroll_tp.cuh), so no sparse indexing happens at run time. Each warp works out of its own shared-memory slice: the problem is split into segments whose irreps and weights fit per-warp shared memory, and 'uvw' paths use a warp-level, register-tiled matmul (wmm.cuh). The fused convolution never materializes per-edge messages; it reduces with atomics, or deterministically over receiver-sorted edges with a transpose permutation for the backward pass, with optional Kahan summation.
when_to_use: Training or running MACE, NequIP, Nequix or SevenNet-style models on NVIDIA or AMD GPUs where e3nn tensor products dominate step time; NequIP documents an OpenEquivariance acceleration path.

Large molecular graphs where unfused e3nn message passing runs out of memory: the docs say the MACE carbon.xyz benchmark (158K edges) needs an 80GB GPU with e3nn, while the fused oeq convolution is expected to fit.
You need an open-source alternative to NVIDIA cuEquivariance (closed-source kernel package), or you need AMD (HIP), JAX or Intel XPU (beta SYCL) support.
Models that need float64 tensor products or higher-order derivatives (forces, force-matching training, Hessian-like terms).
when_not_to_use: Tensor products outside pure 'uvu'/'uvw': mixed instruction types, other connection modes and non-trainable instructions are unsupported. Per a NequIP docs snippet seen in search, Allegro models cannot use it.
CPU-only systems, or nodes with mixed GPU generations: there is no CPU path, and kernels are compiled for the compute capability of the first visible GPU only.
You need an independent head-to-head against FlashTP at high angular momentum: issue #171 asked for one and got no answer, and the '2x over FlashTP' claim is first-party.
MACE symmetric contraction: it is beta, needs e3nn, is not exposed at the package top level, and the docs note user reports of weak backward-pass performance.
AMD GPUs with versions before 0.7.0: a HIP warp-sync bug produced non-conservative forces (issue #211).

integration.form: module (pip package 'openequivariance' plus a C++ extension; kernels are JIT-compiled at first use, with NVRTC on CUDA per issue #162)
integration.dependencies: PyTorch >= 2.4 (>= 2.10 for the precompiled extension, AOTI, export and Intel XPU) or JAX > 0.5.0 with the separate openequivariance_extjax package; CUDA or HIP toolkit, or oneAPI icpx for SYCL; e3nn only for tests, benchmarks and symmetric contraction
integration.min_toolchain: GCC 9+ (c++ --version >= 9.0), Linux, Python with PyTorch or JAX
integration.platforms: Linux GPUs only: NVIDIA (run-tested V100, A100-40/80GB, A5000, T4, H100), AMD (MI250x, MI300x), Intel Data Center GPU Max via beta SYCL; no CPU backend
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; CUDA streams and multiple devices are supported since v0.2.0, and the non-deterministic (atomics) convolution gives run-to-run rounding differences.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — TPProblem mirrors e3nn's o3.TensorProduct (internal_weights=False required) and matches e3nn up to rounding for 'uvu' with multiplicity-1 second inputs; other configurations, including all 'uvw', match only after reordering weights with reorder_weights_from_e3nn/to_e3nn; only 'uvu'/'uvw' are covered

gotchas: The first import builds a C++ extension, which can take minutes; issues #156 and #207 report import hangs on a stale build lock (PR #209 added a timeout), and #175 reports a compilation cache that did not persist on L40S/RTX 6000.
Modules saved after torch.compile or torch.export load only on the same GPU architecture; uncompiled modules recompile kernels when loaded on another GPU.

deterministic=True (the faster, atomics-free convolution) requires edges sorted by receiver, inputs permuted with receiver_perm, and a sender transpose permutation; deterministic=False accepts any order but uses atomics.

Before v0.7.0 the HIP kernels used a block-level thread fence where CUDA used __syncwarp. On an MI300, NequIP-OAM-L (l_max = 3) gave non-conservative forces: 9.3-32.8 meV/A force differences and +79.7 eV/ns NVE energy drift (issue #211, OEQ 0.6.8). It was fixed in PR #217 on 2026-09-10, so upgrade on AMD.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over cuEquivariance when you need open-source kernels, AMD/Intel GPUs, JAX, float64 or the memory-saving fused convolution. Pick cuEquivariance for NVIDIA-only, vendor-supported kernels that also cover Allegro. batmobile reports larger single-kernel gains over e3nn on an RTX 3090 but covers a much narrower set of operations and frameworks.
verified_claims_summary: All headline claims are first-party. The README claims up to 10x over e3nn, with the harness's e3nn baseline compiled by torch.compile max-autotune with CUDA graphs, and parity with cuEquivariance; the docs claim up to 2x over FlashTP's fused kernels, measured on an A100-SXM-80GB at LBNL/NERSC Perlmutter with no compiler or flags stated. The paper abstract (SIAM ACDA25, seen only as search snippets whose figures vary by version) gives up to 4.5-4.8x forward and 3x backward over cuEquivariance, >10x over e3nn and up to 5.3-5.4x MACE inference speedup. One outside data point: the Nequix maintainer reported 2.5x (1000 atoms) and 3.3x (1728 atoms) end-to-end gains from adding the oeq kernels to Nequix's PyTorch port, on an A100 per the thread.
status_note: Actively maintained academic project (v0.7.0 on 2026-09-10, SYCL backend merged 2026-09-23), BSD-3-Clause (LBNL/UC Berkeley) and pip-installable; it ships frequent correctness fixes, so pin a recent version.
